newsitem.title: ZAIRE: PM nomination changes nothing, Zaire rebels say.
newsitem.headline: PM nomination changes nothing, Zaire rebels say.

text.p: Zairean rebels said on Wednesday the nomination of Etienne Tshisekedi by the opposition in Kinshasa as new prime minister made no difference to their goal.

Aid workers meanwhile prepared to repatriate 4,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees after months in the jungles of eastern Zaire and expressed despair for 80,000 more south of the northeastern city of Kisangani.
The opposition in parliament nominated Tshisekedi, President Mobutu Sese Seko's arch-foe, on Tuesday as new prime minister to steer Zaire through negotiations with Tutsi-dominated rebels.
"It won't make any difference. Our purpose is to get rid of Mobutu and we will push until we have got him out," Mwenze Kongolo, justice commissioner in the rebel alliance, told Reuters.
Kongolo said that Tshisekedi, 64, was probably best-known in the capital Kinshasa and his appointment might have some weight there "but the rest of the country is waiting for us".
Many Zairean politicians said they expected ailing Mobutu to move quickly to sign Tshisekedi's appointment into law to succeed prime minister Kengo wa Dondo, who resigned a week ago.

The rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Cong-Zaire warned Tshisekedi against taking the job, arguing anyone under Mobutu can play no part in a rebel-led transitional government which Kabila has called for.

Presidential Movement leader Idambituo Bakata indicated on Tuesday that Mobutu would endorse the appointment of the man he sacked as prime minister in 1992. A sovereign conference reappointed Tshisekedi but Mobutu again dismissed him in 1993.
Tshisekedi has huge popular backing in Zaire but support for rebel leader Laurent Kabila has also grown as rebel forces have seized a quarter of the country since October.
Tshisekedi has long favoured peace talks with Kabila.
Mobutu, suffering from prostate cancer, is sending a seven-man team headed by his security adviser to represent Kinshasa authorities in talks with the rebels in South Africa this week.

Filippo Grandi, head of the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR in Goma, said aid workers were preparing on Wednesday to repatriate up to 4,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees from Karuba in Zaire by truck, having moved 1,500 from there to Rwanda via Goma on Tuesday.
Aid officials said 20,000 refugees remained at Karuba and agencies also planned on Wednesday to empty sites at Tingi Tingi and Amisi of refugees and fly them to Goma for repatriation.

UNHCR spokesman Peter Kessler said the death rate at Tingi Tingi on Tuesday was between 10 and 15 people per day out of 1,000. "This is an unacceptably high rate but people elsewhere are much weaker," he added.
He said aid agency staff clearing shelters at Lula, seven km (four miles) south of Kisangani, found 50 bodies on Monday of refugees who had died from exhaustion, sickness or malnutrition.

The rebels ordered 20,000 refugees to leave Lula on Monday and join another 60,000 farther south of Kisangani for security reasons. The rebels fear they include former Rwandan Hutu troops and militiamen who fought alongside Zairean government troops.
Kessler said 384 refugees had died of hunger, exhaustion and disease at Ubilo, 82 km (51 miles) south of Kisangani since March 16.
"We are also finding very few children under the age of five either because they were abandoned or they just died during the forced marches across the country from the east.
"Some refugees are dying in our trucks as we drive them home. They are dying even while needles are being inserted in their arms to try and keep them alive," he said.
"What we want from the rebels is a response to our plan to mobilise five planes a day to get the most vulnerable out via Kisangani. Shifting people south of Lula is simply inhumane," Kessler added.
He said many were too weak to survive the week-long drive to Rwanda from Kisangani, which fell to the rebels on March 15.
